papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc educational web lesson arguing that integer problems are hard and that integer (including binary) problems map onto its Dirac solvers.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear optimization under linear constraints becomes NP-hard when the variables are restricted to integers, and that this model is known as integer linear programming.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer Optimization, web lesson (single page)
quotes: In fact, they become NP-hard
This is a famous model known as integer linear programming
assertions.certainty_reason: A textbook result stated without proof or citation on the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The NP-hardness of integer linear programming is a standard result, but this page neither proves it nor cites a source.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for continuous variables, interior point methods can solve linearly constrained linear optimization efficiently, in the sense of polynomial time.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer Optimization, web lesson (single page)
quotes: it can be proven that these methods, known as " interior point methods " can solve this kind of problem efficiently in the sense of polynomial time
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the page attributes to a proof elsewhere (a linked lesson), not shown here.

assertions.value: The authors state that rounding a non-integer point can go two ways per variable, that the number of possibilities doubles each time a variable is added (16 directions to round in four dimensions), and that the number of points to check grows exponentially.
assertions.anchor: Section Why is integer hard?, web lesson (single page)
quotes: the number of possibilities doubles each time a variable is added
with 16 possible directions to round
the number of points to check grows exponentially
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative argument for naive rounding, given without a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument covers only exhaustive checking of the points adjacent to a continuous optimum; it is an intuition, not a hardness proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that no known algorithm is efficient for finding the most optimal integer solution, and that finding one would show that P=NP.
assertions.anchor: Section Why is integer hard?, web lesson (single page)
quotes: none that we know of so far are efficient for finding the most optimal solution
if one were found, this would show that P=NP
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of the state of knowledge, without citation.
assertions.reader_inference: The implication holds for NP-hard problems in general; the page states it for integer linear programming without argument.

assertions.value: The authors state that a family of algorithms using clever rounding, known as LP relaxations, provides a powerful class of approximation algorithms.
assertions.anchor: Section Why is integer hard?, web lesson (single page)
quotes: a family of algorithms which use clever rounding are known as LP relaxations and provide a powerful class of approximation algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement without citation or approximation guarantees.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear optimization without additional constraints is either trivial or unbounded.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer Optimization, web lesson (single page)
quotes: Without additional constraints, these problems are either trivial or unbounded.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated with a short informal argument in the text, not a formal proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The page states this for non-negative variables, as set up in the preceding sentences.

assertions.value: The authors state that the equation setting the sum of the cubes of two positive integers equal to the cube of a third positive integer has no solution, and that this can be proven with advanced mathematics.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer problems tend to be harder, web lesson (single page)
quotes: it can be proven that there is no solution
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the page asserts without proof or citation.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the exponent-three case of Fermat's Last Theorem; the page does not name it.

assertions.value: The authors state that finding two factors of a given number is trivial without restrictions but becomes hard when the factors must be integers, and that this hardness is the basis of much of modern cryptography.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer problems tend to be harder, web lesson (single page)
quotes: this problem again becomes hard if we require that X X X and Y Y Y be integers
In fact, this kind of problem being hard is the basis of much of modern cryptography
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement without proof or citation.
assertions.reader_inference: Integer factoring is not known to be NP-hard; the page uses hardness loosely here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cube equation and factoring examples are not optimization problems, though they could be converted to optimization problems, and that integer problems tend to be hard and are therefore a natural paradigm for QCi's solvers.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer problems tend to be harder, web lesson (single page)
quotes: While neither of the problems discussed so far are optimization problems (although they could be converted to optimization problems)
integer problems tend to be hard, and therefore are a natural paradigm for QCi's solvers
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing the fit of its own product to a problem class.
assertions.reader_inference: The page says integer problems tend to be hard; it does not say all instances are hard.

assertions.value: The authors state that a linear inequality constraint has a natural quadratic expression: a squared penalty term with a non-negative slack variable and a large positive constant, which is zero when a suitable slack value exists and otherwise incurs a large penalty.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer linear programming and Dirac, web lesson (single page)
quotes: linear constraints have a very natural quadratic expression
can be found to make the expression zero. But if it cannot, a large penalty is incurred.
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard penalty construction described informally; no bound on the constant is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not say how large the penalty constant must be for the penalized problem to share its optimum with the constrained one.

assertions.value: The authors state that their Dirac hardware is designed to solve quadratic unconstrained problems, that Dirac provides a more powerful model than integer linear programming because the objective can also contain quadratic terms, and that it can implement even higher order interactions.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer linear programming and Dirac, web lesson (single page)
quotes: our Dirac hardware is designed to solve quadratic unconstrained problems
Dirac provides a more powerful model than integer linear programming, since nothing prevents the objective function from also containing quadratic terms.
It can also implement even higher order interactions
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own product; no performance data on the page.
assertions.reader_inference: More expressive is not more efficient; the page gives no solution-quality or speed result.

assertions.value: The authors state that a variable can be limited to a maximum value by adding a single additional slack variable and one squared term.
assertions.anchor: Section Binary problems on a higher-than-binary solver, web lesson (single page)
quotes: We can constrain a variable to take a maximum value of m m m , by adding a single additional variable.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction stated without proof; it follows the slack penalty of the previous section.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a non-negative variable the expression X times the square of (X minus one) is zero if and only if the variable equals 0 or 1, and takes a positive value for other integer points.
assertions.anchor: Section Binary problems on a higher-than-binary solver, web lesson (single page)
quotes: will be zero if and only if X i = 0 X_i=0 X i = 0 or X i = 1 X_i=1 X i = 1
and will take a positive value for other integer points
assertions.certainty_reason: The property follows by direct inspection of the expression, stated with its condition (non-negative variable) in the section.
assertions.reader_inference: The expression is cubic in the variable, yet the page calls the constraint quadratic (it says it can be accomplished with a quadratic constraint if we restrict to integers). The zero and positivity property holds as stated; the quadratic label is the page's wording and does not match the printed degree.

assertions.value: The authors state that a variable can be constrained to binary values without adding a slack variable, so a binary problem with n variables, a QUBO for example, can be mapped to an integer solver with n variables.
assertions.anchor: Section Binary problems on a higher-than-binary solver, web lesson (single page)
quotes: We can therefore constrain a variable to take binary values without adding an additional slack variable.
can be mapped to an integer solver with n variables
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing how problems map onto its own solver.
assertions.reader_inference: The saving counts variables only; the binary-enforcing term has higher degree than the quadratic form the hardware is described as solving, so the claim of no overhead depends on the higher order interactions the page mentions elsewhere.

assertions.value: The authors state that an integer solver can do everything a binary solver can do, plus much more.
assertions.anchor: Section Binary problems on a higher-than-binary solver, web lesson (single page)
quotes: an integer solver can do everything a binary solver can do, plus much more!
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own product class.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that solving problems over an integer domain tends to be harder than over continuous variables, that integer problems are therefore an important and powerful setting for their hardware, and that general integer problems can be restricted to binary using simple constraints without extra variables.
quotes: A key feature of these problems is that it tends to be harder to solve problems over an integer domain rather than continuous variables.
integer solving is an important and powerful setting for our hardware to work in
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor summarizing the fit of its own hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson contains no experiments; every statement is argued informally or stated without citation.
